newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: Pilgrim wrestles with Saudi haj fire's fallout.
newsitem.headline: Pilgrim wrestles with Saudi haj fire's fallout.

text.p: Fifty-year-old Mahmoud, his seamless white robe whipped up by desert winds, recalled the cries of fear as he surveyed the charred debris of a fierce fire that swept through the haj pilgrimage.
"People were crying for help," he said, the emotional toll of the fire that swept through 70,000 white tents in the Mena plain in Saudi Arabia, killing 217 and injuring 1,290, clear on his face.

When Tuesday's rolling inferno finished claiming lives and spreading panic, all he could see was a lone Omani flag over the bare frames of white tents that were once temporary refuge from blistering temperatures to pilgrims from the Gulf Arab state.

Nearby, a Sudanese electrician surveyed the damage of the latest tragedy to shake the haj pilgrimage, a sacred rite that has in the past seen bloody clashes with Iranian pilgrims and a stampede that crushed those seeking to get closer to God.

The pilgrims, who looked past the tragedy towards Mount Arafat where they gathered in swarms on Wednesday to pray in the haj's climax, walked slowly past melted refrigerators, air conditioners, towels and shirts.
They carried on with haj, clutching prayer mats and cool boxes and using umbrellas against the glaring sun.
Some recalled how Saudi police trying to save pilgrims and battle the blaze also fell victim to metres-high orange flames that showed no mercy for haj, one of the five pillars of Islam.
"Police went to see the fire but they were caught up in it. Some were killed, others injured," said one.
Envoys from India to Indonesia charged with finding any bodies of their nationals and carrying out painful logistics were frustrated by a lack of fresh information on casualties.

"All our efforts to get an idea of the number of dead are in vain. Hospital staff are not authorised to speak and Saudi authorities are not sharing new information with the embassies or press," a diplomat said.
State-run Saudi television tried to allay worries by interviewing pilgrims who had nothing but praise for the Saudi government's management of this year's haj.
Saudi army personnel rolled up their sleeves, helping to erect new tents trucked in from Jeddah for pilgrims left without shelter by the flames.

But efforts to revive the spirit of haj were too late for some of the two million faithful -- half of whom travelled to the desert kingdom from abroad for a ritual where everyone from Burmese to Bangladeshis, princes to paupers, walked side by side.

Some pilgrims gave up on achieving one of the five tenets of Islam this year. "We will come next year for haj, because we have lost everything," one Pakistani pilgrim told Reuters of his group of 10 who were turning back to Mecca.
Saudi Arabia, custodian of Islam's two holiest shrines, has spent $18.6 billion in the last decade on expanding pilgrimage sites and officials had vowed to do their best to ensure a safe haj.
But the bulldozers which ploughed through the destruction amid the lingering smell of smoke were a vivid reminder that tragedy can strike at any minute.
